column6: A bias is an unfair lean toward one side. AI learns from data created by people, and people have prejudices. AI copies them, and sometimes amplifies them.

column5: El tema tiene tres preguntas grandes. ¿Con qué obras aprendió la IA? ¿De quién es lo que genera? ¿Puedo imitar el estilo de un artista? Cada país responde distinto, y las reglas siguen cambiando.
column6: The topic has three big questions. Which works did the AI learn from? Who owns what it generates? Can I imitate an artist's style? Every country answers differently, and the rules keep changing.

column5: En Estados Unidos, la Oficina de Derechos de Autor no registra obras hechas solo por IA. En marzo de 2026 la Corte Suprema se negó a revisar el caso Thaler, y la regla sigue: hace falta un autor humano. Si tú aportas creatividad, esa parte sí puede protegerse.
column6: In the United States, the Copyright Office won't register works made solely by AI. In March 2026 the Supreme Court declined to hear the Thaler case, so the rule stands: there has to be a human author. If you add creative input, that part can be protected.

column6: The first question is being fought over: writers, artists and news outlets have sued AI companies for training on their work without permission. One of the best-known cases is The New York Times against OpenAI and Microsoft, filed in 2023.
